    t-SNE, den-SNE and DREAMS¶

    Python port of the R vignettes t-SNE, densMAP and den-SNE and DREAMS. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    The t-SNE family in one place. Plain t-SNE with Barnes-Hut, a quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut and two flavours of FFT-accelerated interpolation. Then the two extensions that fix t-SNE's best known weaknesses: den-SNE keeps relative density, DREAMS keeps the global arrangement.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import openTSNE
import polars as pl
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

import manifolds_rs as mf


def scatter(
    ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks."""
    ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])


def panels(
    embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False
    )
    for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True):
        scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap)
    fig.tight_layout()
    import time import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import openTSNE import polars as pl from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist from scipy.stats import spearmanr from sklearn.decomposition import PCA import manifolds_rs as mf def scatter( ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks.""" ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6) ax.set_title(title) ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) def panels( embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring.""" fig, axes = plt.subplots( 1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False ) for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True): scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap) fig.tight_layout()

    t-SNE¶

    t-SNE models pairwise similarities as a Gaussian in the input space and a Student t in the embedding, then minimises the KL divergence between the two. The heavy tails of the t are the trick: dissimilar points can sit far apart without huge gradients, which is what fixes the crowding problem of earlier methods. Compared to UMAP:

    • Better on continuous structure. The loss is symmetric and driven by pairwise probabilities rather than graph connectivity, so it tears continuous manifolds apart less readily. Not immune though, especially at low perplexity.
    • Slower. Naive t-SNE is O(N^2). Barnes-Hut gets it to O(N log N), the FFT versions to O(N) with a bigger constant.
    • Distances in the embedding mean nothing. Cluster sizes and gaps between clusters should not be over-interpreted.

    Perplexity is the knob: roughly the effective number of neighbours per point. 5 to 50 is the usual range. Low values chase local structure, high values pull in more of the global picture.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000)
X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000)
X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000)
    X_clust, y_clust = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000) X_swiss, t_swiss = mf.datasets.swiss_roll(1_000) X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000)

    Clustered data¶

    Ten Gaussian clusters in 50 dimensions. PCA first, for a baseline.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_clust),
        "t-SNE (Barnes-Hut)": mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0).fit_transform(X_clust),
    },
    y_clust,
)
    panels( { "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_clust), "t-SNE (Barnes-Hut)": mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0).fit_transform(X_clust), }, y_clust, )

    Clean separation, as expected. The gaps between the clusters and their sizes are not something t-SNE tries to get right, so don't read them.

    Swiss roll¶

    A 2-D sheet rolled up in 3-D, coloured by the position along the roll. We need a higher perplexity here to give the global structure a chance, and with 1000 points an exact search costs nothing.

    In [4]:

    panels(
    {
        "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_swiss),
        "t-SNE, perplexity 50": mf.TSNE(
            perplexity=50.0, ann="exhaustive"
        ).fit_transform(X_swiss),
    },
    t_swiss,
    cmap="viridis",
)
    panels( { "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_swiss), "t-SNE, perplexity 50": mf.TSNE( perplexity=50.0, ann="exhaustive" ).fit_transform(X_swiss), }, t_swiss, cmap="viridis", )

    The colour gradient along the roll survives. Not a proper unrolling though: for that, look at PHATE.

    Trajectory¶

    A branching trajectory in 50 dimensions, coloured by branch. The points are shuffled before plotting so the later branches don't hide the earlier ones.

panels(

    t-SNE gets the branches out of the PCA blob, but without knowing the differentiation path you would struggle to read the order off this plot.

    Pre-computed kNN graphs¶

    Sweeping perplexity or epochs? Compute the graph once. t-SNE wants 3 * perplexity neighbours, so the widest perplexity you plan to try sets k. A graph no wider than perplexity is an error; a wider one is used in full, so slice it (idx[:, :3 * perplexity]) to get the default width.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X_clust, k=45, ann="ivf")

panels(
    {
        "perplexity 10": mf.TSNE(perplexity=10.0).fit_transform(
            X_clust, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist
        ),
        "perplexity 15, 300 epochs, lr 100": mf.TSNE(
            perplexity=15.0, n_epochs=300, learning_rate=100.0
        ).fit_transform(X_clust, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist),
    },
    y_clust,
)
    idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X_clust, k=45, ann="ivf") panels( { "perplexity 10": mf.TSNE(perplexity=10.0).fit_transform( X_clust, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist ), "perplexity 15, 300 epochs, lr 100": mf.TSNE( perplexity=15.0, n_epochs=300, learning_rate=100.0 ).fit_transform(X_clust, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist), }, y_clust, )

    The second one stops early with a small learning rate, which is how you get the half-cooked look on purpose.

    The repulsion approximations¶

    The attractive forces only run over the kNN graph and are cheap. The repulsion runs over all pairs and is where the time goes. Four ways to approximate it, picked with approx:

    • "barnes_hut" (default, alias "bh"): a quadtree, O(N log N).
    • "bh_qd" (alias "qd"): the quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut from qdtsne. The tree depth is capped at TsneOptim(max_depth=...) (default 7), and repulsion is computed once per leaf from its centre of mass instead of once per point. A bit less precise, a lot faster. qdtsne recommends depths of 7 to 10.
    • "fft": FIt-SNE. Charges are spread onto an interpolation grid and the repulsion comes out of an FFT convolution. O(N), with a constant that pays off from a few tens of thousands of points.
    • "fft_3k": the three-kernel variant. Put a unit charge on the grid and convolve it with three kernels (q, q^2 dx and q^2 dy), which hands you the normalisation and the forces directly. One forward and three inverse transforms per epoch instead of four and four.
    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    approx = {
    name: mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0, approx=name).fit_transform(X_clust)
    for name in ("barnes_hut", "bh_qd", "fft", "fft_3k")
}
panels(approx, y_clust)
    approx = { name: mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0, approx=name).fit_transform(X_clust) for name in ("barnes_hut", "bh_qd", "fft", "fft_3k") } panels(approx, y_clust)

    Same picture four times. On large data you may see the clusters stop being islands and relax into a gapless disc, tiled into Voronoi-like cells. That is not a convergence failure. The main phase runs at an exaggeration of 1, and at high point density the equilibrium of that setting is space filling. Set TsneOptim(late_exag_factor=...) to 2 to 4 and the gaps come back.

    den-SNE: keeping density¶

    t-SNE carries the same warning as UMAP: cluster sizes in the embedding mean nothing. A blob twice as wide as its neighbour might be ten times tighter in the input. Neither loss has a term that cares how spread out a neighbourhood was to begin with.

    den-SNE adds one:

    \[-\lambda \cdot \mathrm{Corr}(\log R_o, \log R_e)\]

    \(R_o\) is a local radius in the input, a graph-weighted average squared distance to a point's neighbours, and \(R_e\) the matching radius in the embedding. Maximise their correlation and a tight cluster stays tight, a diffuse one stays diffuse. The term only switches on over the last DensParams(frac=...) of the epochs (default 30%), so it corrects a settled layout instead of fighting the initialisation. lambda_ weighs it, and 0 gives you plain t-SNE back.

    To see any of this we need to measure local density before and after. A proxy for \(R_o\): the log of the mean squared distance to the 15 nearest neighbours. The cluster generator draws a different spread per cluster, so there is real density variation to keep.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    def local_radii(x: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> np.ndarray:
    """Log mean squared distance to the `k` nearest neighbours, per point."""
    _, d = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="kmknn")
    return np.log((d.astype(np.float64) ** 2).mean(axis=1) + 1e-8)


X_dens, y_dens = mf.datasets.clustered(10_000, n_clusters=8)
radii = local_radii(X_dens)

pl.DataFrame({"cluster": y_dens, "log_radius": radii}).group_by("cluster").agg(
    pl.col("log_radius").mean().round(2)
).sort("cluster")
    def local_radii(x: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> np.ndarray: """Log mean squared distance to the `k` nearest neighbours, per point.""" _, d = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="kmknn") return np.log((d.astype(np.float64) ** 2).mean(axis=1) + 1e-8) X_dens, y_dens = mf.datasets.clustered(10_000, n_clusters=8) radii = local_radii(X_dens) pl.DataFrame({"cluster": y_dens, "log_radius": radii}).group_by("cluster").agg( pl.col("log_radius").mean().round(2) ).sort("cluster")

    rho is the Spearman correlation between input and embedding radii. Turn lambda_ up if you want more of it; the UMAP vignette sweeps the same knob for densMAP. den-SNE inherits every t-SNE constraint: two dimensions only, a pre-computed graph needs more than perplexity neighbours, and every approx works.

    DREAMS: keeping the global arrangement¶

    t-SNE throws away where the clusters sit relative to each other. DREAMS gets it back with a pull towards a reference layout. Every epoch it scales the usual update by 1 - lambda and adds

    \[-\eta \lambda^2 \frac{2}{n} (y - \alpha y_e)\]

    \(y_e\) is the centred reference, \(\alpha = \|Y\|_F / \|Y_e\|_F\) rescales it to the current size of the embedding, and \(\eta\) is the automatic openTSNE learning rate. The optimisation starts from the reference too, so init is ignored. lambda_ lives in [0, 1]: 0 is t-SNE started from the reference, 1 returns the reference. The default 0.15 is the paper's. The extra term is O(n) per epoch, so DREAMS costs what t-SNE costs, and every approx works.

    Two numbers per embedding. Global: the Spearman correlation between subcluster centroid distances in the input and in the embedding. Local: the fraction of each point's 15 nearest neighbours that survive.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    def global_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, groups: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Spearman correlation of group centroid distances, input vs embedding."""
    ids = np.unique(groups)
    cx = np.stack([x[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids])
    ce = np.stack([emb[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids])
    return float(spearmanr(pdist(cx), pdist(ce)).statistic)


def knn_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> float:
    """Mean fraction of each point's `k` exact neighbours kept in the embedding."""
    a, _ = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="exhaustive")
    b, _ = mf.knn_graph(emb, k=k, ann="exhaustive")
    return sum(len(set(i) & set(j)) for i, j in zip(a, b, strict=True)) / a.size


def scores(x: np.ndarray, embs: dict[str, np.ndarray], groups: np.ndarray):
    """Global and local preservation per embedding, as a table."""
    return pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "method": list(embs),
            "global": [global_preservation(x, e, groups) for e in embs.values()],
            "local": [knn_preservation(x, e) for e in embs.values()],
        }
    ).with_columns(pl.col("global", "local").round(3))
    def global_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, groups: np.ndarray) -> float: """Spearman correlation of group centroid distances, input vs embedding.""" ids = np.unique(groups) cx = np.stack([x[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids]) ce = np.stack([emb[groups == g].mean(axis=0) for g in ids]) return float(spearmanr(pdist(cx), pdist(ce)).statistic) def knn_preservation(x: np.ndarray, emb: np.ndarray, k: int = 15) -> float: """Mean fraction of each point's `k` exact neighbours kept in the embedding.""" a, _ = mf.knn_graph(x, k=k, ann="exhaustive") b, _ = mf.knn_graph(emb, k=k, ann="exhaustive") return sum(len(set(i) & set(j)) for i, j in zip(a, b, strict=True)) / a.size def scores(x: np.ndarray, embs: dict[str, np.ndarray], groups: np.ndarray): """Global and local preservation per embedding, as a table.""" return pl.DataFrame( { "method": list(embs), "global": [global_preservation(x, e, groups) for e in embs.values()], "local": [knn_preservation(x, e) for e in embs.values()], } ).with_columns(pl.col("global", "local").round(3))

    The hierarchical generator gives us 16 subclusters in 4 supergroups, in 50 dimensions. Subclusters within a supergroup are close, supergroups are far apart. Exactly the structure t-SNE throws away.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    X_hier, supergroup, subgroup = mf.datasets.hierarchical(5_000, n_subclusters=4)

hier = {
    "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_hier),
    "t-SNE": mf.TSNE().fit_transform(X_hier),
    "DREAMS": mf.DREAMS().fit_transform(X_hier),
}
panels(hier, supergroup)
scores(X_hier, hier, subgroup)
    X_hier, supergroup, subgroup = mf.datasets.hierarchical(5_000, n_subclusters=4) hier = { "PCA": PCA(2).fit_transform(X_hier), "t-SNE": mf.TSNE().fit_transform(X_hier), "DREAMS": mf.DREAMS().fit_transform(X_hier), } panels(hier, supergroup) scores(X_hier, hier, subgroup)

    Coloured by supergroup. PCA puts the supergroups in the right places and smears the subclusters inside them. t-SNE separates all 16 subclusters and scatters them over the plane with no regard for their supergroup. DREAMS keeps the subclusters apart and the supergroups together. PCA's local score is dismal: two dimensions out of fifty is not enough to keep anyone's neighbours.

    Tuning lambda¶

    A sweep from t-SNE to PCA.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    sweep = {
    f"lambda = {lam}": mf.DREAMS(lambda_=lam).fit_transform(X_hier)
    for lam in (0.0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.5, 1.0)
}
panels(sweep, supergroup)
scores(X_hier, sweep, subgroup)
    sweep = { f"lambda = {lam}": mf.DREAMS(lambda_=lam).fit_transform(X_hier) for lam in (0.0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.5, 1.0) } panels(sweep, supergroup) scores(X_hier, sweep, subgroup)
    Out[12]:
    shape: (5, 3)
    methodgloballocal
    strf64f64
    "lambda = 0.0"0.4710.227

    Even 0.05 buys most of the global structure back. The local score holds up to the default and then drops off fast. Past 0.5 you are looking at a slightly sharpened PCA, and at 1 nothing moves at all: the reference at its initialisation scale. Start at the default; go lower if the subclusters start to touch.

    Bring your own reference¶

    PCA is a fine reference when the global structure is linear-ish. When it is not, pass something better via reference in fit: any (n_samples, 2) array. On a branching trajectory PHATE is the obvious pick.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    X_t5, y_t5 = mf.datasets.trajectory(5_000)
phate_ref = mf.PHATE(k=15).fit_transform(X_t5)

order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_t5))
panels(
    {
        "PHATE": phate_ref[order],
        "t-SNE": mf.TSNE().fit_transform(X_t5)[order],
        "DREAMS, PHATE reference": mf.DREAMS().fit_transform(X_t5, reference=phate_ref)[
            order
        ],
        "DREAMS, PHATE reference, lambda 0.05": mf.DREAMS(lambda_=0.05).fit_transform(
            X_t5, reference=phate_ref
        )[order],
    },
    y_t5[order],
)
    X_t5, y_t5 = mf.datasets.trajectory(5_000) phate_ref = mf.PHATE(k=15).fit_transform(X_t5) order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_t5)) panels( { "PHATE": phate_ref[order], "t-SNE": mf.TSNE().fit_transform(X_t5)[order], "DREAMS, PHATE reference": mf.DREAMS().fit_transform(X_t5, reference=phate_ref)[ order ], "DREAMS, PHATE reference, lambda 0.05": mf.DREAMS(lambda_=0.05).fit_transform( X_t5, reference=phate_ref )[order], }, y_t5[order], )

    The branch order along the stem follows PHATE. Long PHATE tips can tear off into islands at the default lambda_: that is DREAMS itself, the authors' openTSNE fork does the same. A lower lambda_ keeps them in one piece, so on long trajectories go below the default.

    Benchmarks¶

    Against openTSNE, the fastest t-SNE in Python, on all cores. One run each, wall time in seconds. Mind that the epochs differ: openTSNE runs 250 early exaggeration plus 500 iterations, we run 1000 in total.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    def timed(fn) -> float:
    """Wall time of one call, in seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def bench(x: np.ndarray, ours: list[str], open_tsne: list[str]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Wall time of our approximations and openTSNE's on `x`."""
    rows = [
        {
            "method": f"manifolds-rs {a}",
            "seconds": timed(
                lambda a=a: mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0, approx=a).fit_transform(x)
            ),
        }
        for a in ours
    ]
    rows += [
        {
            "method": f"openTSNE {m}",
            "seconds": timed(
                lambda m=m: openTSNE.TSNE(
                    perplexity=30,
                    negative_gradient_method=m,
                    n_jobs=-1,
                    random_state=42,
                ).fit(x)
            ),
        }
        for m in open_tsne
    ]
    return pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))


bench(mf.datasets.clustered(5_000)[0], ["barnes_hut", "bh_qd"], ["bh"])
    def timed(fn) -> float: """Wall time of one call, in seconds.""" start = time.perf_counter() fn() return time.perf_counter() - start def bench(x: np.ndarray, ours: list[str], open_tsne: list[str]) -> pl.DataFrame: """Wall time of our approximations and openTSNE's on `x`.""" rows = [ { "method": f"manifolds-rs {a}", "seconds": timed( lambda a=a: mf.TSNE(perplexity=30.0, approx=a).fit_transform(x) ), } for a in ours ] rows += [ { "method": f"openTSNE {m}", "seconds": timed( lambda m=m: openTSNE.TSNE( perplexity=30, negative_gradient_method=m, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42, ).fit(x) ), } for m in open_tsne ] return pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2)) bench(mf.datasets.clustered(5_000)[0], ["barnes_hut", "bh_qd"], ["bh"])

    On 5k points Barnes-Hut is close to an order of magnitude ahead of openTSNE. The neighbour search, the affinities and the optimisation all run in Rust, with no round trips through Python. At 75k plain Barnes-Hut starts to hurt, and the quick-and-dirty tree keeps up with both FFT versions. If you like t-SNE but thought it was too slow, this is for you.
